# Cashflow Game Manual

<!-- Generated by scripts/manual-markdown.js from src/assets/i18n/cashflow-manual/en.json - do not edit by hand. -->

How to play, every card type, what to buy, and what the numbers say - for Cashflow game accounts.

## 1. Getting started

The Cashflow game is a companion for the board game: you play on the real board with a real die, and this app keeps the books. Everything you do is real bookkeeping in your account - transactions, subscriptions, Grow projects, a balance sheet - so you can see exactly what each decision does to your money.

> **Who can read this** This manual and the game are for **Cashflow game accounts** only: an account whose email address contains the word `cashflow`. Such an account is a dedicated play account - nothing in it is real money, and nothing you do reaches a normal account. The game works the same on the Firebase edition and on a self-hosted server.

1. **Create or sign in to a Cashflow account** - Register with an email address that contains `cashflow`, for example `anna.cashflow@example.com`. The menu then shows a **Cashflow Game** entry with a 🎲.
2. **Open the game and choose a game set** - **Classic Edition** has the 12 professions of the printed game and the complete card piles. **Custom JFK** adds three more professions (software developer, freelancer, entrepreneur) and uses the same card piles.
3. **Pick a profession** - Choose one from the list or press **Shuffle** for a random one. The profession card opens with its printed numbers - income, expenses, savings and debts. Read it before you start.
4. **Press Start game and choose the language** - The app asks which language you want to play in. The cards, the labels of your purchases (SFH, CONDO …) and the notes follow it, and every game remembers its own language.
5. **The game is set up** - The app books your savings as starting cash, creates your monthly salary and every expense as a subscription, and adds the debts of your profession to the balance sheet. The dashboard opens.
6. **Play** - Move your token on the real board. When you land on a space, tell the app which one (see ‘The spaces’). At Payday press **Payday**. That is the whole loop.

> **You decide, the app calculates** The app never takes a decision away from you. It shows what a card costs, how much cash you have, what a bank loan would cost and what a deal pays - and then you press the button or you don’t. A good game is won by reading those numbers before every purchase.

## 2. The goal: out of the rat race

You start with a job that pays for your life and little else. The rat race ends when you no longer need the job.

### Passive income

**Passive income** is the money that comes in every month without your work: the cashflow of the properties and businesses you own. Your **expenses** are everything that goes out every month - taxes, rent or mortgage, loan payments, living costs, the cost of your children and the interest on a bank loan. Your salary is not passive income.

> **You have won the rat race when** **passive income ≥ monthly expenses**. The dashboard then shows a green banner: ‘You escaped the rat race!’ You can keep playing as long as you like - the banner simply disappears again if your expenses rise above your passive income.

### How the game can go wrong

If your **monthly cashflow** (all income minus all expenses) is negative, every Payday takes cash away instead of adding it. The dashboard warns you in red. It does not stop you: sell something, pay off a loan or find a better deal before the next Payday.

> **Debt is not a loss - bleeding is** Owing money is part of the game; a mortgage is how almost every property is bought. What hurts is a monthly cashflow below zero, especially together with an expensive bank loan (10% of the loan every month).

### What you are playing for

- **Get the passive income up** - every property or business you buy adds its cashflow to every future Payday.
- **Keep the expenses down** - babies and bank loans raise them; paying a loan off lowers them again.
- **Do not run dry** - doodads and repair bills arrive without warning, so keep some cash back.

_(Table: How much passive income each profession needs - and roughly how many properties that is - the figures are in the topics cashflow_cards, cashflow_card_lab and cashflow_strategy_lab.)_

## 3. The dashboard

Open the game from the menu and you land on the dashboard. Everything you need during a turn is on this one screen.

| Where | What it shows or does |
| --- | --- |
| Summary card | Your profession (tap the info button to see its card), your **cash**, the game date, your **monthly cashflow** and small badges: children, a running Charity reminder, a Downsized reminder. |
| Banners | Red when your monthly cashflow is negative. Green when passive income covers your expenses - you escaped. |
| **Payday** and **Undo** | Payday books one month. Undo takes back the last step - any step, not only a Payday. |
| Open decision | A card that waits for a dice roll (see ‘Dice cards’) appears here, with a **Roll the dice** button. |
| Which space did you land on? | The coloured buttons: **Deals** (green), **Doodad** (red), **Market** (blue), and purple **Charity**, **Downsized**, **Baby**. |
| Bank loan | **Borrow** and **Repay** your loan in steps of 1.000 (see ‘Bank loans’). |
| My games, History, Menu | Your saved games, the list of every step you took (each can be undone), and a shortcut to the app menu. |

### The profession card

Tap the info button next to your profession to open its card. It has two views you can switch between: **Starting Scenario** (the printed card as you began) and **Live - Current Game** (the same layout with today’s numbers: your income and expenses, the properties you own, your debts).

> **The rest of the app is still there** Your transactions, subscriptions, Grow projects, balance sheet and statistics are the normal pages of the app, filled by the game. Open them from the menu any time - see ‘The game and the rest of the app’.

## 4. Professions

Your profession decides how much you earn, how much you spend, how much cash you start with and what debts you carry. Fifteen are available: the twelve of the printed game and three custom ones.

_(Table: All professions, best monthly cashflow first - the figures are in the topics cashflow_cards, cashflow_card_lab and cashflow_strategy_lab.)_

### What to look at when you choose

- **Cashflow (salary − expenses)** is the money you can invest every month. A bigger number means faster deposits.
- **Expenses** are the target you have to cover with passive income. Small expenses mean fewer properties to escape.
- **Savings** is your starting cash and your first deposit. A profession with low savings starts with small deals.
- **Debts** are paid down from your monthly payments; they are the first mortgage-like costs you carry.
- **Per child** is added every time you land on Baby. It is small for some professions and large for others.

> **High salary is not automatically easy** The doctor earns the most, but also spends the most: 8.300 of expenses have to be covered by passive income. The caretaker needs only 1.000 - one good Big Deal property. A high salary buys deposits faster; low expenses make the finish line closer. Both routes work.

_(Table: Passive income each profession must reach - the figures are in the topics cashflow_cards, cashflow_card_lab and cashflow_strategy_lab.)_

## 5. Payday and the game calendar

Payday is the heartbeat of the game. One press books one month.

### What Payday does

- books your **salary** and the **cashflow of every property and business** you own,
- books every **expense**: taxes, rent or mortgage, loan payments, living costs, children and the interest on your bank loan,
- moves the game calendar on by **one month** and counts the round,
- opens the **dice roll** of any Multi-Level-Marketing card you hold (one roll for all of them),
- ends the **Market offers** you were holding - an offer from a Market card is good until the next Payday only.

Payday never skips. Even with a Charity or Downsized reminder showing, you press Payday every time you pass it on the board. The reminders are for your turns on the physical board, which the app cannot see.

### The calendar

The game has its own calendar that moves one month per Payday. For bookkeeping the transactions are placed inside the **current real month**, each on the day of its subscription (salary early in the month, mortgage on its day …). Purchases and payments you make between two Paydays take the next free day of the month, so the account list stays readable.

> Older game transactions move back one month with every Payday. Statistics therefore show your game as a timeline, and nothing you do here mixes with a real account.

> **Pressed Payday by mistake?** Press **Undo**. It restores everything the Payday changed, including the date. Every other step can be undone the same way - see ‘History, Undo and saved games’.

## 6. The spaces

The app does not move your token - you do, on the real board. When you land on something, you tell the app which space it was and it takes care of the rest.

- **Deals** - Green. Choose the **Small Deal** or the **Big Deal** pile. Stocks, funds, houses, apartment buildings, businesses, gold and some gambles.
- **Doodad** - Red. Something you buy without having planned it (the German card is called Schnickschnack). You always pay.
- **Market** - Blue. An event for the whole table: buyers for your properties and gold, stock splits, repair bills and two star cards.
- **Charity** - Purple. Give a tenth of your income away and roll one or two dice for the next three turns.
- **Downsized** - Purple. Pay all your monthly expenses once and sit out two turns.
- **Baby** - Purple. One more child, one more monthly expense (at most three children).

> **Charity, Downsized and Baby ask first** They show what they will do - with your real numbers - and wait for **Play** or **Cancel**, so a mis-tap changes nothing.

### Finding the card you drew

After you choose a pile you have two ways to bring a card up:

- **Find the card you drew** - you have the physical card in your hand. Type a name, a symbol or a price (for example `OK4U 20`), or use the quick filters (kind, type, account, category) and tap the card in the list.
- **Draw a card** - you have no physical pile: the app draws one at random and does not repeat a card until the pile is used up.

Then the card appears on screen with its text and its numbers, exactly as printed. What you can do with it depends on its kind - the following sections go through them one by one.

> **Wrong card?** Every card has a **Pick another one** (or a back arrow) while you have not played it. Nothing is booked until you press the play button.

## 7. How to invest: plan, buy, sell

Every house, share, business and gold coin you buy is a **Grow project** - the same investment tracker the rest of the app uses. A card turns into a project in three steps.

1. **Plan** - On the card press **Plan this**. A Grow project is created in the **plan** phase with the card’s numbers and a note: what the purchase costs, the cash you have, and the bank loan you would need. Nothing is paid yet.
2. **Buy** - Open the project (the app takes you there) and press **buy**. The Add dialog opens ready to go, on the **Fire** account. Check it and confirm. The project moves to **execute**; a property creates its mortgage in the balance sheet and its monthly cashflow as a subscription that every Payday pays out.
3. **Sell** - Open the project and press **sell** whenever you want out. The sale is booked as income, the mortgage is paid off and the cashflow stops. When everything is sold the project is **completed**.

> **A project for every card** A second house of the same type becomes a second project with a number added to its name: `SFH`, `SFH-II`, `SFH-III`. Each can be sold on its own.

### Not enough cash?

If the deposit is more than your cash, the app takes a **bank loan** for exactly the missing amount - rounded up to the next 1.000 - and books it first, as its own step. The purchase follows as the second step. Undo takes the purchase back first, and the loan with the next Undo. See ‘Bank loans’ for what that costs.

_(Example card: classic-small-efh-45k-2k - A Small Deal card: a single-family home for 45.000 with 2.000 deposit - it pays 250 a month.; see cashflow_cards.)_

### The names of your purchases

Each purchase is named by a short label in the language of your game, so they are easy to tell apart in the lists and charts:

| Type | English label | German label |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Single-family home | SFH | EFH |
| Condo | CONDO | ETW |
| Apartment building (4 / 8 units) | APT4, APT8 | MFH4, MFH8 |
| Semi-detached house | SDH | DH |
| Apartment complex (12 / 24 / 60 units) | CPX12, CPX24, CPX60 | APH12, APH24, APH60 |
| Business partner / automated business / car wash | PTR, ABIZ, WASH | GP, AU, AWA |
| Pizza franchise, gold, multi-level marketing | PIZZA, GOLD, MLM | PIZZA, GOLD, MLM |

> **Sell to a friend** On a Deal card **Sell to a friend** books a one-off sale: you agreed a price with another player and the money comes in at once. **Decline** simply returns to the dashboard.

## 8. Small Deal

The Small Deal pile is for beginners: small prices, small deposits. It has 38 cards - 20 stocks and funds, 11 houses and condos, and 7 special cards (gold, dice gambles and Multi-Level-Marketing).

### Stocks and funds

There are four securities - three stocks and one fund - and five cards for each, one per price. A stock is a **liquidity tool, not passive income**: it pays no monthly cashflow. You buy low, sell high and use the cash for a bigger deposit.

_(Example card: classic-small-ok4u-20 - A stock card: you may buy at this price. The trading range tells you where the price will move.; see cashflow_cards.)_

_(Table: The four securities - the figures are in the topics cashflow_cards, cashflow_card_lab and cashflow_strategy_lab.)_

- **Buy** from the project (you set the number of shares when you plan it); the price of the card is the price you pay.
- **A card for a share you already hold** does not plan a new purchase - it **sets the market price**. The button reads **Update price**; the price changes on your Grow project and on your shares, a note records what happened on the stock market, and you can sell or buy at the new price. Your past sales stay as they were.
- **Stock splits** (Market pile, see ‘Market cards’) double or halve the number of shares you hold.

### Single-family homes and condos

_(Example card: classic-small-etw-55k-5k - A condo with a big mortgage - watch what a buyer would pay for it before you buy.; see cashflow_cards.)_

_(Table: Small Deal properties - the figures are in the topics cashflow_cards, cashflow_card_lab and cashflow_strategy_lab.)_

> **Two cards pay nothing** The 30.000 single-family home and the 40.000 condo with 1.000 deposit have a cashflow of **0**. They are traps: they eat a deposit and give nothing back until a buyer shows up. The table above counts them in the last column.

### Gold, gambles and multi-level marketing

- **Plain gold offers** - 10 coins for 3.000 and 5 coins for 1.000. Coins pay nothing; they are worth what a gold buyer pays (see ‘Market cards’).
- **Dice gambles** - the box of gold, the journey and the sister-in-law’s loan. You pay first and roll a die afterwards (see ‘Dice cards’).
- **Multi-Level-Marketing** - two cards: pay 500 and keep the card; at every Payday you roll a die and a 4–6 pays 500.

_(Example card: classic-small-gold-friend-3000 - Ten gold coins at a bargain price.; see cashflow_cards.)_

_(Example card: classic-small-mlm-1 - A card you keep: it rolls at every Payday.; see cashflow_cards.)_

## 9. Big Deal

Big Deal cards need real deposits - from 10.000 up to 200.000 - and pay real cashflow. There are 36 cards: a pizza franchise, ten apartment buildings, eight single-family homes, five semi-detached houses, four apartment complexes and eight businesses.

_(Table: Big Deal cards by type - the figures are in the topics cashflow_cards, cashflow_card_lab and cashflow_strategy_lab.)_

### Real estate

Houses, apartment buildings and complexes are bought with a mortgage. You pay the deposit; the mortgage becomes a liability in your balance sheet, and the **cashflow on the card is what is left after the mortgage payment** - so it is the number that lands on your Payday.

_(Example card: classic-big-mfh8-240k-40k - An apartment building with 8 units: 40.000 deposit, 1.800 a month.; see cashflow_cards.)_

_(Example card: classic-big-aph12-350k-50k - An apartment complex with 12 units.; see cashflow_cards.)_

### Businesses

The pizza franchise, the business partners, the automated companies and the car wash work like properties: a deposit and a monthly cashflow. Partners are bought outright (no mortgage), the others have one. Businesses are **not** counted as properties by the cards that talk about ‘your property’ - repair bills do not hit them.

_(Example card: classic-big-au-150k-30k-2500 - An automated business: a modest deposit, 2.500 a month.; see cashflow_cards.)_

> **How big is big?** The average Big Deal card pays about ten times the cashflow of the average paying Small Deal card, for a deposit roughly ten times larger. Small Deals build the first deposit; Big Deals end the rat race.

## 10. Dice cards

Some cards are decided by a die. You pay first, then the roll is made - with the app’s die or with your own.

### How a roll works

- After you pay (or play the card) an **open decision** appears on the dashboard.
- **Roll the dice** lets the app roll: a large die is shown, then the result, until you press **Continue**.
- Or roll a real die and report it: **I rolled it: I won** / **I rolled it: no luck** (for a stock split the two buttons read ‘1–3’ and ‘4–6’).
- The result is one step in your History and can be undone - the open decision comes back.

- **What’s in the box?! / Where there’s a will** - Pay 500 (the box) or 750 (the journey). A **6** wins ten gold coins; anything else wins nothing - or an old cat.
- **Sister-in-law borrows money** - Pay 5.000. **1–3**: she never pays you back. **4–6**: she pays back **10.000**. It is fair on average, but you win or lose big.
- **Multi-Level-Marketing** - Pay 500 and keep the card. At **every Payday** one roll for all your cards: **4–6** pays **500** per card. It is the best-paying card in the pile.
- **Stock splits** - A Market card for one company. If you hold its shares: **1–3** doubles them, **4–6** halves them. Price and cost do not change.

_(Example card: classic-small-sister-5000 - Costs 5.000, comes back as 10.000 on a 4, 5 or 6.; see cashflow_cards.)_

_(Example card: classic-small-gold-box-500 - Costs 500, wins ten coins on a six.; see cashflow_cards.)_

> **Reading the odds** A single die has six sides: ‘4–6’ is 50%, ‘6’ is one in six. The chapter on the odds works out what each gamble is worth on average.

## 11. Doodads (Schnickschnack)

The red pile is the price of living: a boat, a night out, a new computer. There are 42 cards and you cannot decline one - you only decide how it is paid.

_(Example card: classic-doodad-boat - A Doodad: the app suggests the account and the category.; see cashflow_cards.)_

1. **Open the card** - Find or draw it. It shows the cost, the account the app suggests and the spending category it will go under.
2. **Add the transaction** - The Add dialog opens filled in: account, amount, today’s free date, the category and a comment with a short joke, what you have in cash and how much bank loan you would need, and the tag `#doodad`. Change anything you like.
3. **Confirm** - If you are short, the app takes the bank loan first (its own step) and then books the payment. Nothing else changes - you own nothing afterwards.

The big, dreamy purchases (a boat, a kitchen, a first car for a child) are suggested on your **Smile** account; the small things on **Splurge**. Neither takes money from your **Fire** or **Daily** accounts. Every card has a category such as Leisure, Home or Events, so your statements show where a game’s worth of Doodads went.

_(Table: Doodads by category - the figures are in the topics cashflow_cards, cashflow_card_lab and cashflow_strategy_lab.)_

> **Do not call it a loss** A Doodad is a cost of living, not a mistake. On average one costs a little under 1.400 - keep a cushion of one or two of those in cash and Doodads never hurt.

## 12. Market cards

Blue cards are events for the whole table. In the app they only matter for you: if a card has nothing to do with what you own, the app tells you it does not apply, and the play is still noted in your History.

_(Table: What the 39 Market cards are - the figures are in the topics cashflow_cards, cashflow_card_lab and cashflow_strategy_lab.)_

### Buyers for your properties

A buyer card makes an **offer** for one type of property. Play it and every property of that type you own gets the offer, with a note in its Grow project; then you sell the ones you want with the normal **sell** button, which is already filled in. The offer lasts until the next Payday, and you may sell as many properties as you like at that price.

> **What you receive** The buyer pays the full price. The mortgage is paid back from it, and what is left is booked as income. For an offer of ‘original price + profit’ that is **your deposit plus the profit**; for a fixed price it is the **price minus the mortgage**.

- **Single-family homes and apartment buildings** - Original price + a percentage of the full cost, or + a fixed amount. The profit is the same for a 4-unit and an 8-unit building.
- **Condos** - A fixed price for the whole condo. If the price is below the mortgage the sale **costs you** money - the app books it as a payment, not income, and takes a loan if you need one.
- **Apartment complexes** - A price **per unit**, times the units of your complex (a 24-unit complex counts 24), minus the mortgage.
- **Gold coins** - Cash for **every coin**. Sell all of them or as many as you like - edit the number in the sell dialog.

_(Example card: classic-market-efh-pct20-a - A percentage buyer for single-family homes.; see cashflow_cards.)_

_(Example card: classic-market-etw-65k - A fixed price for a condo - compare it with the mortgage on your own condo first.; see cashflow_cards.)_

_(Example card: classic-market-gold-central-2k - A gold buyer: every coin at 2.000.; see cashflow_cards.)_

### Repair costs

‘A tenant damages your property’ and ‘Sewer pipe broken’ cost property owners 500 to 2.000 once. If you own no property, you ignore the card. Otherwise the Add dialog opens on **Fire**, filled in with the cost and the name of the first property you own as the category. Businesses are not properties.

_(Example card: classic-market-cost-pipe-2k - Only for property owners.; see cashflow_cards.)_

### Stock splits and star cards

A **stock split** card has the name of one company on it. Without its shares the card does not apply. With them a dice decision opens: 1–3 doubles your shares, 4–6 halves them (rounded in your favour). The price and your costs stay the same.

The two **★ star cards** are the jackpots: ‘Small Business Boom!’ lifts every investment that pays 1.000 or less by 250 a month; ‘New management system’ lifts everything that pays 2.000 or less by 400. Your Grow project and its monthly income are both raised for good, and a note records it.

_(Example card: classic-market-boost-small-250 - A star card: your passive income goes up for the rest of the game.; see cashflow_cards.)_

_(Table: How often a Market card concerns you - the figures are in the topics cashflow_cards, cashflow_card_lab and cashflow_strategy_lab.)_

## 13. Charity, Downsized and Baby

Three spaces that need no card. They ask for confirmation first and show the numbers they will use.

| Space | What it does in the app | What you do on the board |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Charity** | Pays **10% of your total monthly income** (salary plus passive income) once, as a payment on your Daily account. | For your next 3 turns you may roll one or two dice. A badge reminds you; dismiss it yourself when the turns are used. |
| **Downsized** | Pays **all your monthly expenses** once. Also ends a running Charity badge. | Sit out two turns while the others play. A badge reminds you. |
| **Baby** | Adds a child (at most **3**) and a monthly expense for it - the ‘Per child’ amount of your profession - which every Payday pays. | Nothing more. The button is greyed out at three children. |

> **Why Charity can be worth it** Ten per cent of income is usually a small price for two dice on each of three turns: you can move faster to the deal spaces. It is the only space that gives you something back.

> **Downsized when you are tight** It costs the full month of expenses at once. With a small cash reserve it forces a bank loan - take Downsized seriously when you plan your cushion.

## 14. Bank loans

The bank lends in steps of **1.000** and charges **10% of the loan every month**. That is the one rule the app fully automates.

- **Borrow** adds the money to your cash as income, creates a **Bank loan** liability and a monthly expense **Bank loan interest** - a 1.000 loan costs 100 a month, a 5.000 loan 500.
- **Repay** (or **Settle all**) pays the loan back in steps of 1.000. The interest falls with the loan, to nothing when it is gone.
- **Automatic loans** - when a purchase or a payment is bigger than your cash, the app borrows the missing amount, rounded up to 1.000, as its own step in front of the purchase.

> **10% a month is 120% a year** A loan is an expensive bridge, not a way of life. It pays only when the thing you buy with it earns more than 10% of the borrowed money every month. The table below shows which cards manage that.

_(Table: Can the deal pay for its own loan? (monthly cashflow ÷ deposit ≥ 10%) - the figures are in the topics cashflow_cards, cashflow_card_lab and cashflow_strategy_lab.)_

> **Borrow for a moment, repay when you can** A short loan to buy a deal that pays a lot more than the interest is fine. Repay as soon as cash arrives - from a sale, a gold buyer or a lucky roll. While a loan runs it shows as a small bank symbol on your charts.

## 15. The game and the rest of the app

Nothing in the game is a separate system. Every number you see is a normal entry of the Money App - so you can look at it with the normal tools.

| In the game | In the app |
| --- | --- |
| Cash | The sum of your Daily, Splurge, Smile and Fire accounts. Income is split between them by the percentages of your account. |
| Salary, expenses, passive income | **Subscriptions** - one per line. Payday turns them into transactions. |
| Every card you pay or play | A **transaction** in the account it was booked on, with a comment. |
| Houses, shares, businesses, gold | **Grow** projects, and their positions in the **Balance** sheet (assets, shares, investments). |
| Mortgages and bank loan | Liabilities in the **Balance** sheet. |
| Income and expenses by category | The **Income** statement and the account pages - Doodad categories show up here. |
| Your game over time | **Stats**: charts of each account, with markers for Grow trades, Smile and Fire payments, the bank loan and Doodads. |

> **Fire and Smile in the game** Purchases, loans and repair bills run through **Fire**. Dreamy Doodads run through **Smile**, small ones through **Splurge**. That is only the suggestion of the app - you can always book a payment from another account in the Add dialog.

> **Edit with care** You can change entries in the normal pages (a transaction, a subscription, a Grow note). The game does not stop you - but a changed amount changes your monthly cashflow and your rat-race maths. Use **Undo** to take back a step instead of fixing it by hand.

## 16. History, Undo and saved games

Every step you take is recorded, every step can be undone, and an account can keep as many games as you like.

### Undo and History

- **Undo** takes back the last step - a Payday, a card, a loan, a dice roll. Press it again to go further back.
- **History** lists every step in order, newest first, with what it booked. Each line has **Undo back to here**.
- A purchase that needed a bank loan is two steps: the loan, then the purchase.
- A saved game keeps its whole history: after you load it, History lists every move and Undo can walk back step by step, even to before the game started. Games saved before this was added load with an empty history.

### My games

Your account always holds one **live game** - the one you are playing. **My games** keeps the others.

| Button | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| **Save game** | Saves the game you are playing into its slot. A game is also saved automatically when you leave it. |
| **New game** | Saves the live game, then clears the account so you can choose a profession again. |
| **Continue** | Opens a saved game. The game you are playing is saved first, then the other becomes live - cash, projects, notes, even a waiting dice roll. If anything is wrong with the saved game, nothing changes. |
| **Rename**, **Delete** | Rename a game, or delete it for good (with a confirmation). |
| **Export**, **Import game** | Download a game as a file, or add one from a file. A backup, or a way to move a game to another account. |

Each saved game shows its status - **Playing**, **Out of the rat race**, **Bankrupt** or **Ended** - with cash, passive income against expenses and the round, so the list is also a scoreboard.

### Ending a game

- **end game (save it)** (Settings) saves the game with an ‘Ended’ mark and clears the account.
- **reset game** (Settings) deletes the game **without saving** and cannot be undone.

> Saved games live in your own data, next to the rest of your account, compressed and encrypted like everything else. A very long list makes your data bigger - the app warns above 30 games; export and delete the ones you no longer need.

## 17. Strategy

This is the approach the numbers of the card piles support. It is a guide, not a law - the dice and the draw decide a lot.

### 1 · Know your finish line

Your expenses are your target. Look at the ‘passive income needed’ table before the first move and think in properties: one Big Deal property for a caretaker, five for a doctor. Remember that every baby and every bank loan moves the line.

### 2 · Build the first deposit with the small things

- **Multi-Level-Marketing** is the best card in the game: it returns on average 250 a month on 500. If you have the cash, buy it.
- **Small single-family homes and condos with cashflow** give 40–150% a year on a deposit of a few thousand and cost almost nothing to hold. Skip the two that pay nothing.
- **Shares** are cash machines when you buy near the bottom of the range (5–10) and sell near the top (30). They produce no passive income - treat them as deposit money.
- **Gold** is cheap when you buy it from a card and expensive when a gold buyer asks for it: coins from a 3.000-for-10 card sell for 10.000–20.000 on a buyer’s card. The catch is waiting for the buyer (three Market cards in 39).

### 3 · Move to Big Deals as soon as a deposit is affordable

A Big Deal property pays 700–11.000 a month. Two or three of them end the race for most professions. Compare the **return a year** (cash-on-cash) between cards: apartment buildings with 4 units and semi-detached houses are among the highest; businesses bought outright are slower to repay.

> **Deposit first, cashflow second** Two cards can pay the same cashflow with very different deposits. Ask: how many months until the deposit is back? The table of Big Deal types shows the range. A card with a smaller deposit and the same cashflow is the better card.

### 4 · Use loans like a bridge

- Borrow only for a card whose monthly yield is above 10% of the borrowed money - the ‘pays for a loan’ table lists the types that can.
- Never borrow to cover a month you could not afford: if monthly cashflow is negative, a loan only digs deeper.
- Repay the loan from the first cash that arrives. A 5.000 loan costs 500 every month - that is two Multi-Level-Marketing cards’ worth of income.

### 5 · Keep a cushion

Doodads average a little under 1.400, repair bills reach 2.000, Downsized costs a month of expenses. A cushion of 1.500–3.000 in cash keeps those from becoming loans.

### 6 · Diversify against the Market

Holding both single-family homes and apartment buildings means more Market cards help you. Holding only semi-detached houses means no buyer card ever applies, while repair bills do. The ‘how often a Market card concerns you’ table shows it.

### 7 · Sell when a buyer overpays

A buyer offering 20% on top, or a fixed profit of 10.000–20.000, often beats a year of the property’s cashflow. Selling and re-buying a better card can raise your passive income - but remember a sale also removes the cashflow.

> **Common mistakes** Borrowing for a card that pays nothing. Spending the cushion on a share and then meeting a Doodad. Taking a loan at 10% a month for a deal that returns 5%. Selling a condo to a buyer at a price below its mortgage.

## 18. What thousands of simulated games show

The app played whole games by itself - with the same rules and the same cards as yours, thousands of them, for every profession and for several strategies. Nothing below is opinion: it is counted. When a card or a rule changes, the numbers are measured again.

### How to read the numbers

- **Winning** means escaping the rat race: passive income covers every monthly expense. **Losing** means bankruptcy: the monthly cashflow turns negative.
- A **roll** is one turn. Two rolls make about one month (one Payday), so 80 rolls are about 40 months.
- Every strategy plays **the same dice**, so the differences between strategies are not luck.
- The strategies are listed below. Each decides only what you decide too: which pile to draw from, whether to buy the card, whether to borrow, whether to sell to a buyer and whether to repay the bank. Doodads are always paid and Market cards are always played.

### Which strategy wins and how often

_(Table: Every strategy, averaged over all professions - the figures are in the topics cashflow_cards, cashflow_card_lab and cashflow_strategy_lab.)_

- **Never invests** - pays every Doodad, passes every deal: the salary alone.
- **Properties from cash** - buys any property it can pay the deposit for, Small Deals only, never borrows.
- **Picky properties** - only properties paying at least 3% a month on the deposit, keeps 2.000 in reserve.
- **Small first, Big when rich** - Small Deals until cash reaches 20.000, then Big Deals.
- **Borrow when it pays** - borrows the shortfall when a property pays at least 1,5 times the interest the loan adds, repays when it can.
- **Leveraged, Big Deals** - aims at Big Deals from the start and borrows whenever the property pays at least the interest.
- **Marketing first, then properties** - buys every Multi-Level-Marketing card it can afford, then properties from cash.
- **Trade stocks for deposits** - buys stocks at 10 or less, sells at 25 or more, to raise deposit money.
- **All-rounder** - properties above 2% a month, a reserve, loans only when well covered, Multi-Level-Marketing, stock trading, selling to generous buyers, Big Deals once cash allows.
- **Best found by the search** - the best of 216 combinations of those settings that were each played thousands of times (see the report in the project documentation). "Best" means best of what was tried.

### Profession by profession

_(Table: The best and the worst strategy for each profession, and how fast the best one escapes - the figures are in the topics cashflow_cards, cashflow_card_lab and cashflow_strategy_lab.)_

### Every strategy on every profession

_(Table: Share of the games that escape - the figures are in the topics cashflow_cards, cashflow_card_lab and cashflow_strategy_lab.)_

### The highest passive income

_(Table: How much passive income a game can reach, by profession - the figures are in the topics cashflow_cards, cashflow_card_lab and cashflow_strategy_lab.)_

### What stands out

- **Doing nothing loses.** Without investing, about two games in three end in bankruptcy and the rest never escape: a salary does not carry babies, Doodads and the loans they force.
- **Borrow carefully rather than never.** The strategies that borrow only when a card clearly pays for the interest escape about as often as the cautious ones - in roughly half the rolls.
- **Switch to Big Deals once the cash allows.** In the searched settings, going for Big Deals from about 20.000 cash escapes in about half the rolls of the same settings with Small Deals only.
- **Multi-Level-Marketing earns its place.** Every one of the best searched strategies buys it.
- **The highest passive income and the safest escape are different games.** Borrowing heavily for Big Deals reaches by far the largest passive income - one game passed 60.000 a month - but about two games in three end in bankruptcy first.
- **Trading stocks for deposit money did not help** in these measurements: it escaped less often than buying properties from cash alone.
- **The salary decides the odds.** The lowest salaries (caretaker, truck driver) escape in roughly seven games out of ten with the best strategy; pilot, doctor and lawyer escape in practically every game.

> **How far to trust it** These are counts of simulated games, not a proof. A real player decides with more information than a fixed strategy - which card is in front of you, how the others are doing - and the dice still decide a lot. Use the numbers to see which habits tend to win, not to predict one game.

## 19. Odds and numbers

Everything below is read from the card piles themselves, so it is exactly what the game uses.

### What a random draw gives you

_(Table: Chance of each kind of card on a random draw - the figures are in the topics cashflow_cards, cashflow_card_lab and cashflow_strategy_lab.)_

In the Small Deal pile one draw in two is a stock card; in the Big Deal pile, nearly two in five are an apartment building or complex. Doodads are always a cost and have no good outcome - there are 42 of them and the average is a little under 1.400.

### Gambles - what they are worth on average

| Card | You pay | You get | Average result |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Multi-Level-Marketing (per Payday) | 500 once | 50% × 500 per roll | +250 a month - pays back in two Paydays |
| Sister-in-law borrows money | 5.000 | 50% × 10.000 | 0 - a fair coin that doubles or loses |
| What’s in the box?! | 500 | 1/6 × 10 coins | 1⅔ coins ≈ 1.667 at 1.000 a coin |
| Where there’s a will | 750 | 1/6 × 10 coins | the same coins, a higher price |
| Stock split (if you hold the share) | nothing | 50% × 2 shares + 50% × ½ shares | +25% in the number of shares |

The only gamble that is better than fair on its own is Multi-Level-Marketing. Stock splits help the holder (+25% shares on average); the sister-in-law’s loan is fair, so take it only when you can afford to lose 5.000.

### How often the Market helps or hurts you

_(Table: Market cards that concern each kind of asset - the figures are in the topics cashflow_cards, cashflow_card_lab and cashflow_strategy_lab.)_

### The rat race in numbers

An average Big Deal property pays about 1.800 a month; an average paying Small Deal property about 180. To cover 1.000 of expenses you need one Big Deal property or six small ones. The caretaker’s +600 a month alone would take years to save the 32.000–40.000 deposit - which is why the small, quick deals, the gamble cards and the share trades matter at the start.

_(Table: Passive income needed per profession - the figures are in the topics cashflow_cards, cashflow_card_lab and cashflow_strategy_lab.)_

## 20. All the cards

Every card of every pile, to read and search - you cannot play them here. Each card shows its **id**: the game's History names a card you picked by that id, so a game can be looked at afterwards and what you passed on (or rightly left) can be told.

> **Why the ids matter** Every card you pick - drawn at random, or found among your physical cards - is written into the History with its exact id. When a game is analysed, the analyst reads those ids to see which deal you passed on, and plays both choices out many times. **Open the card before you pass it** and the analyst can say whether it was a deal worth taking. Browsing is not tracked, only the card that is open when you act on it or decline it; passing without opening any card is allowed, and the analyst only notes, as a small minus, that you did not look.

_(Every card with its id: topic cashflow_cards.)_

An agent reads the same list from `GET /api/v1/game/cards` (it needs no running game: pass `gameSetId=cashflow`) and from `docs/domain/CASHFLOW_CARDS.md`.

## 21. What the cards are worth

Every card of the game, measured. 142 real positions - taken out of simulated games at roll 3, 10, 20 and 32, for every profession - were each played out 20 times with the card taken and 20 times without it, on the same dice. What a card does is the difference in how often the game escapes the rat race, in **points** (percentage points). A card that helps by 3 points helps a lot in some positions and does nothing in others; an average of many positions is what you can lean on.

> **How to read the tables** Plus helps, minus hurts. "Taken" means a Deal bought, a Doodad paid or a Market card played, and every game after it is played by the all-round strategy of the strategy lab. **From cash** counts the positions where the deposit was in cash on hand, **with a loan** those where the bank had to lend it. The measuring error is about one point for the Small Deals and the Doodads. A built-up game is one deep into the game with properties already owned (the best strategy found, roll 20 to 60).

### Small Deals

The best Small Deal is the **Multi-Level-Marketing** buy-in: **+6 points** and about five rolls saved, for 500 €. Next come the **single-family homes with a 2,000 € deposit** (+3 points from cash, about eight rolls saved) - and the surprise: when the bank has to lend that deposit, they are worth **+10 to +12 points**, because a property that pays 200 to 250 € a month for 2,000 € is worth borrowing for. Condos and the expensive houses (4,000 to 5,000 € deposit) are the other way round: from cash they do roughly nothing, with a loan they cost 10 to 19 points. **Shares** are small bets either way (between −2.5 and +1.5 points): buying half of your cash in shares that you then hold ties it up, and the cheap ones (5, 10 or 20 €) cost slightly more than the dear ones.

_(Table: Every Small Deal, the best to buy first - the figures are in the topics cashflow_cards, cashflow_card_lab and cashflow_strategy_lab.)_

### Big Deals

A Big Deal is a question of **where the deposit comes from**. Bought from cash, the good ones save 5 to 12 rolls (the 10,000 € apartment building and the 10,000 € semi-detached house the most). Bought with a loan they are the single most dangerous thing in the game: **−9 to −84 points** (most of them between −20 and −65), because the loan's interest and the mortgage eat what the property pays. The Pizza franchise and the big apartment complexes are at the bottom of the table (−77 to −84 points with a loan): the deposit is far more than a game at that stage holds. The one exception is the **semi-detached house for 10,000 €** (1,100 € a month): worth buying even with a loan (+3.6 points).

_(Table: Every Big Deal - the figures are in the topics cashflow_cards, cashflow_card_lab and cashflow_strategy_lab.)_

### Doodads: what they cost you

A Doodad is paid, whatever it says - so the question is only how much it hurts. **Each 1,000 € of a Doodad costs about 3.5 to 4.5 points** of the chance to escape: the 7,500 € kitchen takes 34 points, the 5,000 € car or boat 23, a 1,000 € doodad 3.5 and anything under 300 € about one. The same Doodad costs **one and a half to two times as much in the early game** as in the late game - and in a built-up game about half as much, because the properties pay it back sooner. In 6 of 10 bankruptcies the last thing that happened was a Doodad (see below).

_(Table: Every Doodad, the worst first - the figures are in the topics cashflow_cards, cashflow_card_lab and cashflow_strategy_lab.)_

### Market cards

Most Market cards do nothing to you. A **buyer** for your single-family home is worth the most when it offers a fixed amount on top: +20,000 € is worth **4.7 points** (15 rolls saved), +5,000 € only 1 - and +10% not much more than that. The two **business boom** cards (+250 € and +400 € on a business) are worth 2.6 and 3.2 points, and about 12 and 17 rolls in a built-up game. The cost cards (tenant, pipe) cost 0.7 to 3.5 points, about what the same money costs as a Doodad. Stock splits do not matter.

_(Table: The Market cards that touch you - the figures are in the topics cashflow_cards, cashflow_card_lab and cashflow_strategy_lab.)_

### Dice cards: what a gamble costs

A dice card wins on its number or higher: a 4 wins half the time, a 6 one time in six. **The Multi-Level-Marketing buy-in wins half the time and pays every month**: +6 points. **The gold boxes** (a 6 wins, one in six) are small bets that mostly lose: −0.6 and −1.7 points - the coins are worth little compared with what the same money earns in a property. **The sister-in-law** pays 10,000 € back for 5,000 € half the time: on average that is exactly zero, and still it costs 7.6 points - 0.6 when the 5,000 € were in cash, 11.7 when the bank had to lend them: a fair gamble is not free, because the money is gone from the properties it could have bought.

_(Table: The cards decided by a die - the figures are in the topics cashflow_cards, cashflow_card_lab and cashflow_strategy_lab.)_

### Where a game stands on the way

Passive income as a share of the expenses is the figure that tells how near the exit is. The first table shows, per profession, where the games that **did escape** stood at roll 10, 20, 30, 40 and 60 - the middle game, and in brackets the fast tenth and the slow tenth. At roll 20 a game that escapes has typically covered 7 to 24% of its expenses; at roll 40 20 to 60%.

_(Table: Passive income as a share of the expenses, games that escaped - the figures are in the topics cashflow_cards, cashflow_card_lab and cashflow_strategy_lab.)_

The second table turns it round: of all games that stood in a band at that roll, how many escaped and how many went bankrupt. **Being behind early is not lost** (4 in 5 games that have under 5% at roll 10 still escape) - but being behind late is: under 5% at roll 30 leaves two in three, under 5% at roll 60 only 63%. A game that has reached 20% by roll 30 almost always escapes (99%), and from 40% on it is as good as certain.

_(Table: Chance to escape / go bankrupt, by how far a game has got - the figures are in the topics cashflow_cards, cashflow_card_lab and cashflow_strategy_lab.)_

### What ends a game in bankruptcy

Of 12,000 games with the all-round strategy, 16% went bankrupt. The table shows what the last decision before the end was and which cards were most often among the last three. It is **almost always a Doodad** (61%), a Deal that was passed (26%, the game was already lost) or a Market cost card. The kitchen, the first car, the braces and the boat are the most frequent - the expensive Doodads in the deck. The best protection is not a clever Deal but **cash on hand for the next Doodad** (see section 17).

_(Table: The last decision before a bankruptcy - the figures are in the topics cashflow_cards, cashflow_card_lab and cashflow_strategy_lab.)_

> **How the analyst uses this** When a game is analysed, a card you passed on is judged by playing both choices out on the same dice, and set beside these figures: **a Deal you left that was worth +5 points was a miss, one that would have hurt was rightly left**. The analyst also tells you where your game stood at roll 10, 20, 30, 40 and 60 against the games in the second table, and how those ended.

## 22. Questions and answers

Short answers to the things people ask first.

- **Do I need the physical board?**: The app is a companion for it: it keeps the books, the cards and the numbers. You move your token and roll your dice on the board. For the dice cards the app can roll for you.
- **Can I use my normal account?**: No. The game is for accounts with ‘cashflow’ in the email address, and it uses the whole account as the game. A personal account stays untouched by it.
- **Does it work on the self-hosted server and on Firebase?**: Yes, in both. The game and its saved games are stored with your other data; the card texts load on demand.
- **I made a mistake - how do I fix it?**: Press Undo. Every step - a Payday, a card, a loan, a sale - can be undone, and History lets you go back several steps at once.
- **What happens when my monthly cashflow is negative?**: Each Payday takes cash instead of adding it, and the dashboard shows a red warning. Sell something, repay a loan or find a better deal. The game does not stop.
- **What is the Fast Track?**: The second phase of the board game after you escape the rat race. The app does not play it yet - you can carry on in the rat race as long as you like.
- **Why did the app take a bank loan on its own?**: A purchase or payment was bigger than your cash. It borrows exactly the missing amount, rounded up to 1.000, as a separate step - undo it if you would rather decide yourself.
- **A card I own a copy of is missing - where is it?**: The piles are complete: Small Deal 38, Big Deal 36, Doodad 42, Market 39. Use the search on the pile screen and the quick filters.
- **I played in one language and now the app is in another**: Each saved game remembers its language and switches to it when you continue the game, so labels like SFH or EFH stay consistent.
- **Where is the manual in my language?**: The manual is written in English and German so far. Other languages show the English version.

## 23. Glossary and quick reference

The words of the game in one place.

- **Rat race**: The first phase: a job that pays your living costs and nothing more. You leave it when passive income covers your expenses.
- **Passive income**: The monthly cashflow of your properties and businesses - money that arrives without your work.
- **Cashflow**: Income minus expenses, per month. On a card, the monthly money the investment pays after its mortgage.
- **Payday**: The step that books one month of salary, passive income and expenses.
- **Deposit (down payment)**: What you pay yourself for a property. The rest is the mortgage.
- **Mortgage**: The part of a property financed by a lender. It becomes a liability; its payment is already inside the card’s cashflow.
- **Return a year (cash-on-cash)**: Twelve months of cashflow divided by your deposit.
- **Small Deal / Big Deal**: The two green piles. Small Deal: low prices, stocks, small properties, gold and gambles. Big Deal: large properties and businesses.
- **Doodad (Schnickschnack)**: A red card: an unplanned expense. You always pay.
- **Market card**: A blue card: an event for everyone - buyers, repair bills, stock splits, boosts.
- **Star card ★**: A rare Market card that raises your passive income for good.
- **Grow project**: The tracker for an investment: plan, execute, completed. Every card you buy lives in one.
- **Open decision**: A card that waits for a dice roll on the dashboard.
- **Offer**: What a Market buyer pays. Good until the next Payday.
- **Live game**: The game your account is playing right now. Saved games are copies that can become live again.
- **Bank loan**: Money from the bank in steps of 1.000 at 10% of the loan per month.
- **Fire / Smile / Splurge / Daily**: The four spending accounts of Money App. In the game, purchases go through Fire, dreamy Doodads through Smile, small ones through Splurge.
